questions.question: What is the conditional expectation $E[X\mid B]$?
options: The probability that $X$ equals event $B$
The variance of $X$ before observing $B$
The expectation of $X$ given that $B$ occurred.
The largest possible value of $X$ inside $B$.
questions.explanation: $E[X\mid B]$ is the expectation of $X$ computed under the conditional probability model in which $B$ has occurred.
questions.source_support: The definition says it is the expectation computed under the conditional probability model in which $B$ has occurred.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $X$ is a number and $B$ an event, so '$X$ equals $B$' is not meaningful.
That describes a variance, not a conditional mean.
It is an average over $B$, not the largest value in $B$.

questions.question: What condition is required on the event $B$?
options: $B$ must be the whole sample space
$B$ must be independent of $X$
questions.explanation: Conditional expectation $E[X\mid B]$ requires $P(B)>0$ so that the conditional probability model $P(\cdot\mid B)=P(\cdot\cap B)/P(B)$ is defined.
questions.source_support: The definition assumes $B$ is an event with $P(B)>0$.
option_explanations: $P(B)=0$ leaves the conditional model undefined, since $P(\cdot\mid B)$ would divide by zero.
$B$ need not be the whole sample space; any event with $P(B)>0$ (e.g. 'machine failed') supports conditioning.
$B$ need not be independent of $X$; conditioning is most useful precisely when $B$ and $X$ are dependent.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Why is $E[X\mid B]$ not defined in the usual event-conditioning way if $P(B)=0$?
options: The conditional probability model given $B$ is not defined
The expectation of every random variable is zero
The event must contain every outcome
The variance becomes negative
questions.explanation: If $P(B)=0$, the conditional probability $P(\cdot\mid B)=P(\cdot\cap B)/P(B)$ divides by zero, so the conditional model is undefined and $E[X\mid B]$ is not defined in the event-conditioning sense.
questions.source_support: The definition requires $P(B)>0$.
option_explanations: It is not true that every expectation becomes zero; the expectations themselves are fine, only $E[X\mid B]$ is undefined.
$B$ need not contain every outcome; in fact if $B$ contained every outcome then $P(B)=1\neq 0$, the opposite of the hypothesis.
The variance does not become negative; variance is always non-negative, and the issue is undefined conditioning, not variance.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
